one_liner: Google's pure-Go gRPC; beat a stock gRPC C++ async server at 2-4 CPUs in one grpc_bench run, lost in another.
what_it_does: grpc-go (module google.golang.org/grpc) is the Go implementation of gRPC: a client (ClientConn with name resolution, load balancing and xDS support) and a server that runs handlers generated by protoc-gen-go-grpc, over its own HTTP/2 transport built on golang.org/x/net's framer and HPACK encoder. It is a Go API, not a C++ library; it speaks the gRPC wire protocol, so a Go server can replace a C++ server process behind the same .proto. Server.ServeHTTP can also mount gRPC inside net/http, but the code comments say that path uses Go's separate HTTP/2 server and may differ in performance and features.
how_it_is_fast: Each connection has a reader goroutine and a 'loopy writer' goroutine that drains a control buffer, interleaves DATA frames from active streams within flow-control quota, and batches frames into a 32 KB write buffer that it flushes only when nothing is queued; if fewer than 1,000 bytes are pending it yields once (runtime.Gosched) so stream goroutines can add to the batch (internal/transport/controlbuf.go). Every RPC runs in its own goroutine on Go's netpoller-backed M:N scheduler, so all GOMAXPROCS threads share incoming calls instead of being bound to one completion queue each as in the C++ async example used as the baseline. A BDP estimator sizes flow-control windows dynamically, and buffers come from a mem.BufferPool. The measured lead is a scaling effect, not per-core speed: at 1 server CPU it is 0.97x of C++.
when_to_use: Any Go service that needs gRPC: it is the reference Go implementation and is wire-compatible with C++, Java, Rust and .NET peers.
Small unary RPCs on 2-4 core containers, where the 2026 grpc_bench run put it at 88,531-117,082 req/s against 74,869-85,485 for the stock gRPC C++ async servers (1.18-1.37x).
Memory-constrained deployments: 21-31 MiB average memory in grpc_bench #559, similar to the C++ servers (9-32 MiB) and far below grpc-dotnet (122-135 MiB) or Java Vert.x (108-333 MiB).
Services that need xDS, ALTS, interceptors or OpenTelemetry stats in the same library (all live in this module and its go.mod).
when_not_to_use: If you need a stable speed advantage over C++ gRPC: the 2022 run of the same harness reversed the order (1.28x at 1 CPU, 0.73x and 0.85x at 2-3 CPUs), a 2025 third-party run (#547) is a tie, and a tuned C++ server (many pre-posted requests per completion queue, callback API, a current gRPC core) was never measured.
Single-core servers with tight tail latency: at 1 CPU it serves 0.97x of cpp_grpc_mt with a p99 of 37.04 ms versus 21.81 ms.

If you want the fastest gRPC server outright: in the same 2026 run rust_tonic_st (102,754 req/s at 1 CPU, 1.85x), grpc-dotnet, rust_thruster and java_vertx_grpc (130,000-153,000 req/s at 2-4 CPUs) all beat go_grpc at every CPU count.

GC-sensitive hot paths: the server path still allocates per RPC (performance issue #3305, 'reduce garbage allocations in server path', open since 2020) and the default server starts one goroutine per stream.
C or C++ codebases: there is no C/C++ API; the only route is a separate Go process.

integration.form: module (Go module google.golang.org/grpc; code generation with protoc-gen-go and protoc-gen-go-grpc)
integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/net (HTTP/2 framer, HPACK), google.golang.org/protobuf, genproto rpc status; go.mod also pulls Envoy go-control-plane, cncf/xds, OpenTelemetry and go-spiffe for the xDS and stats packages
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.26 at HEAD (go.mod 'go 1.26.0'; the benchmarked v1.79.3 needed Go 1.24); the README supports only the two latest Go major releases
integration.platforms: any Go target; the README installs it with a plain import and go build, no C toolchain step
integration.thread_safety: ClientConn and generated clients are safe to share across goroutines; on one stream only one goroutine may call SendMsg and one RecvMsg at a time; each server handler runs in its own goroutine (Documentation/concurrency.md)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: wire-compatible with gRPC C++ (same .proto, same HTTP/2 protocol), so it can replace a C++ server or client process, but it is not a C++ library and shares no API or ABI

gotchas: Baseline asymmetry in the measured win: the C++ servers link Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++-dev (unpinned; Debian stable ships the 1.51.1 series per Debian package listings seen in a search snippet, so most likely a late-2022 gRPC core) while go_grpc used grpc-go v1.79.3 from 2026. cpp_grpc_mt is the helloworld async pattern with one completion-queue thread per GRPC_SERVER_CPUS and a single pre-posted RequestSayHello per queue, so under 1,000 concurrent requests each queue accepts new calls one at a time. Its efficiency collapses with cores, from 57,403 req/s at 103% CPU to 85,485 at 406% (about 55,600 to 21,100 req/s per CPU, derived from page data), while go_grpc goes from 55,667 at 101% to 117,082 at 333% (about 55,200 to 35,100). The 2-4 CPU win therefore measures a poorly scaling C++ server, not faster per-core code.

bench.sh limits the server with docker --cpus, a CFS quota rather than a cpuset: go_grpc imports go.uber.org/automaxprocs, so GOMAXPROCS matches the quota, while the C++ process still sees all 16 host cores. Only one run per setting, the client reaches the server through Docker's published port 50051, and the workload is a single unary complex_proto echo.

The benchmarked v1.79.3 predates three 2026 advisories: GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset mitigation bypass, fixed in 1.82.1), GHSA-vp52-pcj8-j9qc / CVE-2026-84304 (heap exhaustion from millions of tiny DATA frames, fixed in 1.83.1 with receive-buffer compaction) and GHSA-2v4p-qf9q-27wj (xDS server crash on missing :authority and Host, fixed in 1.82.2 and 1.83.2). The fixes add per-frame accounting, and HEAD also turns on the shared write buffer by default (off in v1.79.3); nobody has re-measured throughput on these versions.

Defaults matter: the harness uses grpc.NewServer() with no options, so NumStreamWorkers (experimental, reuses goroutines instead of one per stream), WriteBufferSize/ReadBufferSize and window sizes were not tuned on the Go side either. The faster go_vtgrpc rows (4-8% above go_grpc) come from the vtprotobuf codec, listed separately in wave 2.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick grpc-go when the service is written in Go; tonic and Thruster (Rust) and grpc-dotnet out-served it at every CPU count of the same 2026 run (rust_tonic_st 102,754 vs 55,667 req/s at 1 CPU; grpc-dotnet 123,609-136,452 vs 88,531-117,082 at 2-4 CPUs). Against grpc-dotnet it uses a quarter to a sixth of the memory (21-31 MiB vs 122-135 MiB).
verified_claims_summary: grpc_bench discussion #559 (maintainer run, 2026-04-22, commit c4c93b3, Xeon Gold 6548N, Ubuntu 24.04, ghz client on 11 CPUs, 50 connections, 1,000 concurrent requests, 120 s after 30 s warmup, one run per setting): go_grpc (grpc-go v1.79.3 built with Go 1.26.2, default options) served 55,667 / 88,531 / 109,481 / 117,082 req/s at 1-4 server CPUs against the best C++ server (cpp_grpc_mt or cpp_asio_grpc, app code built with g++ 15.2 -O3 -flto over Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++) at 57,403 / 74,869 / 81,581 / 85,485, i.e. 0.97x, 1.18x, 1.34x and 1.37x (derived from page data). The 2022 wiki run (Xeon E5-1650 v3, grpc-go v1.36.0, Go 1.17) reversed this: 1.28x at 1 CPU, 0.73x and 0.85x at 2-3 CPUs.
status_note: Actively maintained by the gRPC team (latest release v1.84.0 dated 17 Sep on the releases page, 23.1k stars, 120 open issues, Apache-2.0) and the standard choice for Go; the speed edge over C++ gRPC is run-dependent and rests on an untuned, probably 1.51-era C++ baseline, and production users should run 1.84.0 or later because the benchmarked v1.79.3 is affected by 2026 DoS advisories.
